anatomy.lede: A basket star is a small central disc with arms that fork again and again, until the animal becomes a living net nearly a metre wide.

hotspots.label: Central disc
hotspots.text: All the arms grow out of a small central disc. Food caught by the arms is passed back here to the mouth.

hotspots.label: Arm base
hotspots.text: Near the disc the arms overlap one another. This may create turbulence that helps the outer branches catch food or brings more food within reach.

hotspots.label: Forking arm
hotspots.text: Each arm divides again and again into finer branches. Among brittle stars, only the order Euryalida has branching arms.

hotspots.label: Fine branchlets
hotspots.text: The finest branches make a small-meshed net that can catch a wide range of prey.

hotspots.label: Grasping bands
hotspots.text: Raised bands of pedicellariae, tiny grasping structures used for catching prey, ring the arms and give them a banded look.

hotspots.label: Coiled tip
hotspots.text: The tips can coil tightly. When a branchlet touches food, the smallest branches curl around it into a ball that is passed to the mouth.

senses.lede: A basket star responds to light, touch and the flow of water, and decides from moment to moment whether to feed.

senses.name: Light
senses.text: Shine a torch on a feeding basket star at night and it slowly curls up, taking several minutes to become a fist-sized bundle.

senses.name: Touch
senses.text: When a branchlet touches a food particle, the smallest branches close around it, catching animals as large as small shrimps and juvenile fish.

senses.name: Current
senses.text: It feeds only when conditions suit, turning its arms to face the current at moderate speeds and keeping them folded when the flow is too strong.

body.lede: Branching arms and grasping bands are rare among brittle stars. In basket stars they work together as a net that catches food against the current.

systems.title: More arm, same five rays
systems.text: Echinoderms are built on five rays. Some increase the length of their food-gathering arms by adding extra rays, but basket stars branch the original five instead, as only suspension feeders do.

systems.title: Grabbers for catching prey
systems.text: Every member of the basket star's family, the Gorgonocephalidae, has pedicellariae on its arms, and in this family they are used mainly or only for catching prey.

systems.title: Why branch?
systems.text: Branching may help gorgonocephalid basket stars use their pedicellariae to catch zooplankton on the upstream side, unlike unbranched relatives that catch food downstream on mucus-covered tube feet.

mind.lede: The basket star follows a daily routine: hiding by day and climbing high to feed at night.

studies.title: A night-time climber
studies.text: It is nocturnal. At night it climbs to the top of large corals or sea fans, holding on with the lower parts of its arms, and spreads the rest in a bowl shape to catch plankton.

studies.title: Hiding by day
studies.text: By day it curls into a tight ball and retreats to the base of its coral or sea fan, or into a crevice, protecting itself from predators.

studies.title: A matching lodger
studies.text: The shrimp Periclimenes perryae often lives on the giant basket star, and larger shrimps are usually coloured to match their host.
